definition: Martin v. Hunter’s Lessee, 14 U.S. 304 (1816), is a Supreme Court case establishing the Supreme Court’s authority over state courts in matters of federal law. The plaintiff in this case, Martin, and Hunter's Lessee (defendant) had a dispute regarding the ownership of land in Virginia. The Virginia Court of Appeals decided in favor of Hunter’s Lessee, but the U.S. Supreme Court reversed this holding. The Virginia Court of Appeals rejected the U.S. Supreme Court’s reversal by arguing that Section 25 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 (a law that granted the United States Supreme Court appellate review power over state-court decisions) was unconstitutional. The Virginia Court of Appeals reasoned that, under the principle of dual sovereignty, both State and Federal Supreme Courts were most powerful in their own governments with neither having superiority over the other. The United States Supreme Court reconsidered the case, and rejected Virginia's argument that state courts were independent of Supreme Court review on questions of federal law, upholding the Judiciary Act. While states retained sovereignty in many areas, federal law and the federal judiciary were supreme in matters arising under the U.S. Constitution, federal laws, and treaties. Questions of federal law were within the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction. The Court interpreted Article III's grant of judicial power over all cases arising under federal law as permitting Supreme Court appellate review of state court decisions involving federal questions. This case established the U.S. Supreme Court as the final authority on questions of federal law and Constitutional interpretation. By confirming the constitutionality of Section 25 of the Judiciary Act of 1789, the Court ensured that state court decisions involving federal questions could be reviewed by the Supreme Court, promoting uniformity in the interpretation of federal law throughout the nation. Later, in the case Murdock v. Memphis, 87 U.S. 590 (1874), the Court clarified that the appellate review of state court decisions is limited to federal questions, and does not extend to purely state-law issues.
